concepts_used: Composition of the Supreme Court: Strength and Appointment Mechanism

solution.concept_anchor: Parliament fixes SC judge strength, not Constitution
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students associating a constitution with foundational numbers assume the original text permanently fixed the strength, when Article 124 only set a floor.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Article 124 does not permanently fix the number at 8; it only prescribed a starting number 'until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number'.
Eliminate (c): There is no constitutional provision empowering the President alone to alter judicial strength.
Eliminate (d): The Supreme Court has no power to increase its own sanctioned strength.
Confirm (b): The Constitution explicitly delegates the power to fix and expand SC strength to Parliament by law.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who know the original Constitution had 8 judges (including CJI) often assume this number is constitutionally entrenched. The trap lies in the belief that a constitutional matter must be amended by a constitutional amendment. Article 124 uses the phrase 'until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number,' meaning ordinary legislation — not a constitutional amendment — suffices to raise the strength. The current sanctioned strength of 34 (including CJI) was achieved through successive Parliamentary acts, not constitutional amendments.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 124 of the Constitution establishes the Supreme Court but deliberately leaves the question of judge strength to Parliament rather than fixing it permanently. The original Constitution prescribed a strength of 8 judges (1 CJI + 7), but authorised Parliament to increase this by ordinary legislation.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Fixing the number at 8 permanently misreads Article 124, which treats 8 as only the initial number.
• Option (b) — Correct: Parliament has the authority to increase the strength by statute; the current sanctioned strength is 34 judges including the CJI.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The President has no unilateral power to alter the sanctioned strength of the SC.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Supreme Court cannot modify its own composition.

Value Addition:
• The strength was raised from 8 to 11 in 1956, then progressively to the current 34 by the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019.
• This is an ordinary law requiring simple majority, not a constitutional amendment.
• Parliament's power here is a key example of constitutional flexibility on structural matters.

concepts_used: Qualifications and Eligibility for Supreme Court Judges

solution.concept_anchor: Three eligibility routes under Article 124(3)

statement_analysis.statement: A person who has been a judge of a High Court for at least five years is eligible for appointment to the Supreme Court.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 124(3)(a) explicitly prescribes five years as a judge of one or more High Courts as a qualifying route.

statement_analysis.statement: A person must be at least 45 years of age to be appointed as a judge of the Supreme Court.
statement_analysis.reason: The Constitution prescribes no minimum age for appointment to the Supreme Court; only the retirement age of 65 years is fixed under Article 124(2).

statement_analysis.statement: A person who, in the President's opinion, is a distinguished jurist is eligible for appointment even without judicial or Bar experience.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 124(3)(c) provides this third route; it is the President's subjective opinion that determines eligibility, though this route has never been used in India.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) appeals to students who conflate SC eligibility with that of other constitutional posts (e.g., minimum age for HC judges in some discussions), making the fabricated age requirement seem plausible.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Five years as HC judge is expressly stated in Article 124(3)(a) — mark as correct.
Statement 2: No minimum age exists for SC appointment under any constitutional provision; the retirement age of 65 is not an entry qualification — mark as incorrect.
Statement 3: The distinguished jurist route under Article 124(3)(c) requires no HC or Bar experience, only Presidential opinion — mark as correct.
Only statements 1 and 3 are correct, pointing to option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a classic plausibility trap. Many students, aware that various constitutional offices have minimum age requirements, extend this logic to SC judges. The Constitution prescribes a minimum age for the President (35 years), Vice-President (35 years), and Governor (35 years), but deliberately omits any minimum age for Supreme Court judges. A student recalling '45 years' may confuse this with HC judge conventions or foreign jurisdictions.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 124(3) prescribes three distinct eligibility routes for SC appointment: (a) HC judge for five or more years, (b) HC advocate for ten or more years, or (c) a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion. Critically, no minimum age is prescribed.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Five years as an HC judge is the first route under Article 124(3)(a).
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: No minimum age exists constitutionally; only the retirement ceiling of 65 years under Article 124(2) is specified.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The distinguished jurist route under Article 124(3)(c) is constitutionally valid though never invoked in India's history.

Value Addition:
• The 'distinguished jurist' route exists in practice in the UK and USA; its unused status in India is a frequent discussion point.
• The HC advocate route requires 10 years of practice (not continuous service).
• Citizenship of India is mandatory under Article 124(3); no domicile or birth-in-India requirement exists.

concepts_used: Appointment of CJI and the Collegium System

solution.concept_anchor: Collegium composition SC vs HC — NJAC 2015

statement_analysis.statement: The collegium for recommending appointments to the Supreme Court consists of the Chief Justice of India and the three senior-most judges of the Supreme Court.
statement_analysis.reason: The SC collegium comprises the CJI and the four (not three) senior-most SC judges, as established by the Third Judges Case (1998).

statement_analysis.statement: The National Judicial Appointments Commission was declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court primarily because it violated the doctrine of separation of powers and judicial independence, which are part of the basic structure.
statement_analysis.reason: While judicial independence and basic structure were grounds, the NJAC (99th Amendment) was struck down in 2015 (Fourth Judges Case/NJAC case) — 'Fourth Judges Case' is the correct label; 'separation of powers' alone is not the complete ground. More precisely, it was struck down on grounds of judicial independence as part of basic structure; the phrasing in the statement conflates two distinct doctrinal grounds and is misleading — but more importantly, the court that struck it down was the Supreme Court, not a constitutional bench of seven judges as is sometimes misremembered. However, the more testable error here is that the collegium number in Statement 1 is wrong (3 instead of 4).

statement_analysis.statement: The Constitution of India expressly requires that the seniormost judge of the Supreme Court shall be appointed as the Chief Justice of India.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 124 is completely silent on the seniority convention for CJI appointment; the convention is a constitutional practice, not a constitutional mandate.

solution.strong_distractor: a — A student who knows that the NJAC was struck down and that judicial independence is part of basic structure may accept Statement 2 as correct and choose an option excluding only Statement 1 and 3, missing that Statement 2 also contains distortions.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: The SC collegium is CJI + 4 senior-most judges (not 3); the HC collegium is CJI + 2 — this statement swaps the HC number into the SC context, making it incorrect.

Statement 2: The Constitution does not expressly require seniority-based CJI appointment anywhere in Article 124 — this is a convention, not a constitutional text mandate; Statement 3 is therefore also incorrect.
All three statements are incorrect, pointing to option (d) as the answer to 'which are NOT correct'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the entity-swap trap by replacing '4' with '3' — students aware of the collegium system know 'CJI plus some senior judges' but confuse the SC collegium (CJI + 4) with the HC collegium (CJI + 2). Statement 3 is a classic trap: the seniority convention is so entrenched that students treat it as a constitutional provision. The supersession of Justice H.R. Khanna in 1977 demonstrates it is only a convention, breachable by the executive.
solution.final_explanation:
The collegium system evolved through three landmark cases. The Third Judges Case (1998) settled that the SC collegium for recommending SC appointments comprises the CJI and the four senior-most SC judges, while the HC collegium is CJI + 2.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: '3 senior-most judges' is wrong; the correct number is 4.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 124 is silent on the seniority convention; it is constitutional convention, not constitutional text. The NJAC was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015 (Fifth Judge's Bench) on grounds of judicial independence as basic structure.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: No constitutional provision mandates seniority for CJI appointment; the supersession of Justice Khanna in 1977 showed this convention can be violated.

Value Addition:
• The First Judges Case (1981) held 'consultation' with CJI is not binding.
• The Second Judges Case (1993) elevated CJI's opinion to primacy ('concurrence').
• The NJAC (99th Constitutional Amendment, 2014) was struck down in October 2015 in the Fourth Judges Case (NJAC case).

concepts_used: Removal of Supreme Court Judges: Impeachment Process

solution.concept_anchor: Impeachment grounds, majority, and investigation sequence

statement_analysis.statement: The grounds for removal of a Supreme Court judge under Article 124(4) are proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 124(4) explicitly specifies these two grounds; no other grounds for removal exist constitutionally.

statement_analysis.statement: An address for removal must be passed by both Houses of Parliament by a special majority of two-thirds of members present and voting, with no requirement of an absolute majority of total membership.
statement_analysis.reason: The special majority under Article 124(4) requires BOTH a majority of total membership AND two-thirds of members present and voting in each House — both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Judges Inquiry Act 1968, an investigation by a committee is conducted before, not after, the Houses pass the address for removal.
statement_analysis.reason: The statutory procedure requires a three-member investigation committee (comprising SC judge, HC CJ, and a distinguished jurist) to inquire into charges before Parliament proceeds to vote on the address.

statement_analysis.statement: Justice V. Ramaswami was the first Supreme Court judge to face impeachment proceedings, and the motion against him was successfully passed in the Lok Sabha.
statement_analysis.reason: The motion against Justice V. Ramaswami (1993) failed in the Lok Sabha because the ruling Congress party abstained, and no SC judge has been successfully impeached to date.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Three correct statements seems plausible to students who know the grounds and investigation sequence but miss that the absolute majority condition is also mandatory alongside the two-thirds requirement.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Article 124(4) lists exactly 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity' — correct.
Statement 2: The majority requirement is conjunctive — both absolute majority of total membership AND two-thirds present and voting; omitting the first condition makes this incorrect.
Statement 3: The Judges Inquiry Act 1968 mandates investigation before the address — correct.
Statement 4: The Ramaswami motion failed in Lok Sabha (Congress abstained); no judge has been successfully impeached — incorrect.
Two statements (1 and 3) are correct, pointing to option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is designed around the scope-extension trap: students know '2/3rd of members present and voting' is required and may overlook the additional requirement of a majority of total membership. The UPSC has repeatedly tested conjunctive majority requirements where candidates omit one limb. Statement 4 exploits temporal-swap: students know Ramaswami faced proceedings but often misremember the outcome, assuming that reaching the floor vote means it succeeded.
solution.final_explanation:
The impeachment process for SC judges under Article 124(4) is among the most rigorous removal mechanisms in the Constitution. The grounds are limited to proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 124(4) specifies exactly these two grounds.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The special majority requires BOTH (i) majority of total membership and (ii) two-thirds of members present and voting in each House — both conditions are mandatory.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Under the Judges Inquiry Act 1968, a three-member committee investigates charges before Parliament votes on removal.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The 1993 Ramaswami motion failed in Lok Sabha when the Congress party abstained; no SC judge has ever been successfully removed.

Value Addition:
• The investigating committee under the Judges Inquiry Act has one SC judge, one HC Chief Justice, and one distinguished jurist.
• Even if both Houses pass the address, removal requires Presidential approval.
• The Rajya Sabha passed the Ramaswami motion; failure in Lok Sabha ended proceedings.

concepts_used: Original Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (Art. 131)
Inter-State Water Disputes and Exclusion from SC's Original Jurisdiction

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 131 exclusive federal jurisdiction vs. Art. 262 water dispute exclusion
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify both A and R as factually accurate may jump to (a) without examining whether water dispute exclusion causally flows from Art. 131's general scope, when in fact it flows from Art. 262.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion correct? Yes: Article 131 gives the SC exclusive original jurisdiction over Centre-State and State-State disputes, meaning no other court including HCs can hear such cases.

Step 2 — Is Reason correct? Yes: Inter-state water disputes are excluded from SC's original jurisdiction because Article 262 specifically empowers Parliament to bar SC jurisdiction over such disputes, and the Inter-State Water Disputes Act 1956 has done so.

Step 3 — Does R explain A? No: The Reason (water disputes are excluded) is a specific exception to, not a causal explanation of, the general rule stated in A (Art. 131 exclusive jurisdiction). R describes a limitation on A, not the rationale for A's existence. A is true independently of R.
Both A and R are correct but R does not explain A — correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The assertion-reason trap here is subtle: both facts are correct, and both relate to the same jurisdiction topic, making (a) feel natural. However, R describes a carved-out exception — inter-state water disputes excluded from Art. 131 — while A states the general rule of exclusive jurisdiction. An exception to a rule is not a causal explanation of why the rule exists. The jurisdictional authority of Art. 131 exists because of the constitutional design of federal dispute resolution, not because water disputes are excluded.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 131 grants the Supreme Court exclusive original jurisdiction over constitutional disputes between the Centre and States or between States inter se. This exclusivity means High Courts have no concurrent authority over such federal disputes.

A — Correct: Article 131's exclusivity is well-established; no HC can adjudicate a genuine Centre-State constitutional dispute.
R — Correct: Article 262 empowers Parliament to exclude SC jurisdiction over inter-state water disputes, and the Inter-State Water Disputes Act 1956 has effected this exclusion. Once a tribunal is constituted, the SC cannot be directly approached.
Causal relationship: R does not explain why A is true. A exists because the Constitution designed the SC as the federal dispute-resolution forum. R is a specific statutory exception carved out of that general jurisdiction — a limitation on A, not its rationale.

Value Addition:
• Water dispute tribunal awards have the same force as SC decrees under Art. 262.
• Private parties cannot invoke Art. 131 — only the Centre and State governments.
• Art. 131 excludes disputes relating to pre-Constitution treaties and matters governed by other constitutional provisions.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

Reason (R): Inter-state water disputes are excluded from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Article 262, and once a tribunal is constituted under the Inter-State Water Disputes Act 1956, parties must approach the tribunal rather than the Supreme Court.

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect
(d) A is incorrect but R is correct

concepts_used: Writ Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (Art. 32) vs. High Court (Art. 226)

solution.concept_anchor: Evolution of writ jurisdiction — Art. 32 as fundamental right itself
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students may place the 44th Amendment (1978) before the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) if they confuse the amendment number with chronological order, or misremember when basic structure doctrine was applied to Art. 32.
elimination_logic: The Constitution came into force in 1950 with Art. 32 as a FR — this must be first.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic structure doctrine, under which Art. 32 was recognised as unamendable — this is second.
The 44th Amendment (1978) inserted the protection that Arts. 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even under Art. 359 — this reinforced Art. 32's significance and comes third.
The Supreme Court's expansion of PIL under Art. 32 developed through the 1980s (S.P. Gupta 1981, Bandhua Mukti Morcha 1984) — this is fourth.
Correct order: I → II → III → IV, option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 32's status as a Fundamental Right itself evolved through constitutional history rather than being a static provision.

Correct chronological order:
I. Constitution in force (1950): Art. 32 inserted as FR; Dr. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul of the Constitution'.
II. Kesavananda Bharati case (1973): Art. 32 implicitly protected as part of basic structure — cannot be abrogated by amendment.
III. 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978): Explicitly barred suspension of Arts. 20 and 21 under Art. 359, strengthening the Art. 32 framework.
IV. PIL expansion (1980s): SC liberalised locus standi under Art. 32, allowing public-spirited persons to file petitions — judicial innovation beyond constitutional text.

Why other orders fail: Placing III before II ignores that the 44th Amendment's protection was a legislative response to Emergency-era judicial developments catalysed by constitutional interpretation.

Value Addition:
• Art. 32 can be suspended under Art. 359 during National Emergency (unlike Arts. 20 and 21 post-44th Amendment).
• Art. 226 (HC) has wider subject-matter scope but is not itself a Fundamental Right.
• The right to move the SC under Art. 32 cannot be waived by a party.

III. The 44th Constitutional Amendment barred the suspension of Articles 20 and 21 even during a National Emergency, reinforcing the Article 32 framework

concepts_used: Appellate Jurisdiction: Constitutional, Civil, and Criminal Appeals
Special Leave Petition (Art. 136): Scope and Limitations

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 136 SLP — discretionary residual jurisdiction vs. Art. 134 criminal appeal
solution.strong_distractor: b — A student who knows Art. 134 provides criminal appeals to the SC may apply it here, missing that Rajeev's case (acquittal reversed to less than 10 years) falls outside Art. 134's automatic right and must use the discretionary SLP route.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Art. 132 is for constitutional appeals involving substantial questions of law as to constitutional interpretation — Rajeev's case involves no constitutional question, only a criminal conviction.
Eliminate (b): Art. 134 gives an appeal as of right only when HC reverses acquittal to death sentence, or imposes 10+ years imprisonment; Rajeev received 7 years — below both thresholds.
Eliminate (c): Art. 133 governs civil appeals; this is a criminal matter.
Confirm (d): Art. 136 SLP is the residual, discretionary provision that allows the SC to entertain any appeal from any court order — this is the correct route when no other appellate right exists.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the conflation of Art. 134 criminal appeal (available as of right for death sentence or 10+ year imprisonment) with the general SLP route. Rajeev's 7-year sentence does not meet Art. 134's threshold. Students who remember '134 = criminal appeals to SC' without recalling the specific sentence thresholds will choose (b). The scenario is designed to make (b) feel correct by emphasising the criminal nature of the dispute.
solution.final_explanation:
The appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is distributed across several articles, each with specific preconditions. Understanding when a right of appeal exists versus when only a discretionary remedy is available is critical.

Applicable principle: Art. 136 SLP is the residual extraordinary jurisdiction that fills gaps left by Arts. 132–135. It is purely discretionary — the SC may or may not grant leave.

Scenario analysis: Rajeev was acquitted by the Sessions Court. The High Court reversed this and sentenced him to 7 years. His options are:
• Art. 132: No constitutional question involved — inapplicable.
• Art. 133: Civil appeal route — inapplicable to a criminal matter.
• Art. 134: Criminal appeal as of right exists only if HC reverses acquittal to death sentence OR imposes 10+ years. Rajeev received 7 years — both thresholds missed.
• Art. 136 SLP: The correct remedy. SC has discretion to grant or refuse leave.

Value Addition:
• Art. 136(2) explicitly excludes armed forces tribunal orders from SLP jurisdiction.
• Once SLP is granted, it converts into a regular appeal — different procedural consequences apply.
• The 30th Amendment (1972) removed the value-of-subject-matter requirement from Art. 133 civil appeals.

Rajeev was tried before a Sessions Court on charges of grievous hurt causing death. The Sessions Court acquitted him. Which of the following provisions most appropriately governs his remedy?

(a) Article 132, as the High Court's judgment involves a substantial question of law to be interpreted by the Supreme Court
(b) Article 134, since it provides for criminal appeals from High Court judgments to the Supreme Court as a matter of right
(c) Article 133, as all appeals from High Court judgments in original proceedings lie under this provision
(d) Article 136, since this provision covers discretionary appeals where no other right of appeal is available under Articles 132 to 135

concepts_used: Advisory Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (Art. 143)

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 143 — SC may refuse advisory opinion except pre-Constitution matters
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know the SC declined the Ayodhya reference in 1993 may think 'disputed facts' is a distinct general principle, making (c) look like the odd one out, when in reality it is a specific application of the SC's general discretion to decline.
elimination_logic: Identify what three items share: Under Art. 143, the President may refer questions of public importance and the SC's opinion is non-binding, SC may decline to answer in Category 1 references, and the SC's advisory opinion is not a binding precedent — all relate to the general/discretionary advisory jurisdiction.
Identify the odd item: Pre-Constitution treaties and agreements fall under Category 2 of Art. 143, where the SC MUST give its opinion — the SC has no discretion to decline.
The odd one out is (b): it describes the mandatory advisory category, while the others describe the discretionary or non-binding features of Art. 143.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The two-category distinction within Art. 143 is rarely taught in full detail. Students who know 'SC's opinion under Art. 143 is not binding' generalise this to ALL references, missing that pre-Constitution treaties constitute a mandatory category where the SC cannot decline. This distinction has been the basis of at least one UPSC-style question in the past and remains a high-probability trap.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 143 creates the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, but it contains an internal distinction between two categories of references.

• Option (a) — Shares the common feature: The President's advisory reference under Art. 143 produces a non-binding opinion — correct general principle.
• Option (b) — Does NOT share: References concerning pre-Constitution treaties or agreements fall under the mandatory category where the SC MUST give its opinion; it cannot decline. This is the odd one out.
• Option (c) — Shares the common feature: The SC exercised its discretion to decline the 1993 Ayodhya reference — this is consistent with the general discretionary nature of advisory jurisdiction.
• Option (d) — Shares the common feature: Advisory opinions under Art. 143 are not treated as binding judicial precedents under Art. 141.

Value Addition:
• India's advisory jurisdiction differs from the USA, where the SC has no such jurisdiction at all.
• The SC has issued advisory opinions on matters like sea-bed mining rights and the Delhi Laws Act.
• Advisory opinions may be withdrawn or modified in subsequent judicial proceedings.

meta.subject: Polity
concepts_used: Law of the Land: Art. 141 and Binding Nature of SC Decisions

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 141 binding scope — ratio decidendi vs. obiter dicta; SC vs. tribunals

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 141, the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within the territory of India, including the Supreme Court itself in subsequent benches of equal or smaller strength.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 141 binds all 'courts' but the Supreme Court is not bound by its own decisions — a larger bench can overrule a smaller bench's precedent. The statement incorrectly extends Art. 141's binding effect to the SC itself.

statement_analysis.statement: The binding effect of Article 141 extends to the ratio decidendi of a Supreme Court judgment but not to observations made obiter dicta.
statement_analysis.reason: It is settled law that only the ratio decidendi — the legal principle necessarily decided — constitutes the binding law under Art. 141; obiter dicta are persuasive but not binding.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Art. 141 binds 'all courts' and that SC decisions bind all courts below may accept Statement 1 without noticing it incorrectly extends the binding effect to the SC itself.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Art. 141 binds 'all courts in India' — but the SC itself can overrule its own decisions through a larger bench; it is not self-bound. The statement adds 'including the Supreme Court itself' which is factually wrong — Statement 1 is incorrect.
Statement 2: The ratio/obiter distinction under Art. 141 is settled constitutional law — Statement 2 is correct.
Only Statement 2 is correct — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 commits the scope-extension error by adding 'including the Supreme Court itself' to Art. 141's binding scope. Students who remember that Art. 141 binds 'all courts' often overlook the equally important principle that the SC is not bound by its own decisions and can revisit them through a larger constitutional bench. The doctrine of prospective overruling (Golak Nath, 1967) is the most prominent example of the SC departing from its own earlier ruling.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 141 is one of the most impactful provisions in the Constitution, making SC decisions the supreme law of the land for all courts.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: While Art. 141 binds all courts, the Supreme Court itself is not bound by its own decisions. A larger bench can overrule a smaller bench's precedent. The doctrine of prospective overruling (Golak Nath case) and the practice of referring matters to Constitution benches confirm this.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The binding law under Art. 141 is the ratio decidendi — the legal reasoning essential to the decision. Obiter dicta (remarks made in passing) carry persuasive value but are not binding.

Value Addition:
• Art. 141 has been held to bind tribunals as well, not just courts strictly defined.
• Prospective overruling allows SC to change law without disturbing past transactions.
• A five-judge Constitution Bench is needed for Art. 145(3) substantial constitutional questions.

concepts_used: Review Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (Art. 137)

solution.concept_anchor: Curative Petition — Rupa Ashok Hurra case 2002
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students may confuse the Curative Petition with the Review Petition, knowing both relate to post-judgment remedies, and select 'Review Petition' which is the procedural predecessor to a Curative Petition.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): A Writ Petition is an original petition, not a post-judgment remedy against an SC order.
Eliminate (c): A Review Petition is the remedy immediately preceding a Curative Petition — after review is dismissed, only then is a Curative Petition maintainable.
Eliminate (d): A Special Leave Petition is a pre-judgment discretionary remedy, not a post-review remedy.
Confirm (b): The Curative Petition, established in the Rupa Ashok Hurra case (2002), is the post-review remedy heard by a bench of three senior-most judges plus the bench that decided the review.
solution.final_explanation:
The Supreme Court's hierarchy of post-judgment remedies flows from Art. 137 (Review) to the judicially created Curative Petition. The Curative Petition was established in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002) as the final recourse after a review petition is dismissed.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: A Writ Petition under Art. 32 is an original action for FR enforcement, not a post-judgment remedy.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Curative Petition lies after review is exhausted; it is heard by a bench of the three senior-most SC judges plus judges who decided the review petition.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: A Review Petition under Art. 137 precedes the Curative Petition; once review fails, only then can a Curative Petition be filed.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: An SLP is filed before a final judgment, not after review is exhausted.

Value Addition:
• Curative Petitions are very rarely entertained; they must show a violation of natural justice or that a judge had a conflict of interest.
• Review petitions are typically heard in chambers without oral arguments.
• Both Review and Curative remedies are SC-specific; HCs have review powers under Art. 226 but no curative petition equivalent.

concepts_used: Court of Record Status and Contempt Powers (Art. 129)

solution.concept_anchor: Contempt of Courts Act 1971 — truth as defence added 2006
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the Contempt of Courts Act is from 1971 may accept any pairing involving 1971 without scrutinising the year in which 'truth as defence' was added, confusing the Act's enactment year with the amendment year.
elimination_logic: Evaluate (a): Article 129 does declare the SC a Court of Record with inherent power to punish contempt of itself — this pairing is factually correct.
Evaluate (b): The truth defence was added to the Contempt of Courts Act by a 2006 amendment, not by the original 1971 Act — this pairing is incorrect.
Evaluate (c): Article 215 (not Article 226) gives the HC court-of-record status and contempt powers — incorrect pairing.

Evaluate (d): Civil contempt involves wilful disobedience of court orders; criminal contempt involves scandalising the court or interfering with administration of justice — these definitions are swapped in option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) exploits the temporal-swap trap by substituting 1971 (the year the Contempt of Courts Act was passed) for 2006 (when 'truth as a defence' was added by amendment). Students who recall '1971 Act' without knowing the subsequent 2006 amendment will mark (b) as correct. This amendment was added following public debate about whether truth-telling could be punished as contempt.
solution.final_explanation:
The contempt power of the SC and HC derives from their court-of-record status, independently supplemented by the Contempt of Courts Act 1971.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: Article 129 explicitly declares the SC a Court of Record and confers the inherent power to punish contempt of itself.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: Truth as a valid defence in contempt proceedings was introduced by the 2006 amendment to the Contempt of Courts Act, not by the original 1971 legislation.
• Option (c) — Incorrectly matched: It is Article 215, not Article 226, that gives the HC its court-of-record status and contempt power. Article 226 relates to writ jurisdiction.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: Civil contempt is wilful disobedience of court orders; criminal contempt involves scandalising the court, prejudicing judicial proceedings, or interfering with justice — the definitions are transposed.

Value Addition:
• Both SC (Art. 129) and HC (Art. 215) are courts of record with contempt powers.
• SC's contempt power is not subject to any legislative limitation under the Contempt of Courts Act.
• A High Court's records are admissible as evidence and cannot be questioned before any subordinate court.

concepts_used: Transfer of Cases and Judges: Arts. 139A and 222

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 139A case transfer vs. Art. 222 judge transfer — distinct provisions

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 139A, the Supreme Court may transfer cases involving the same or substantially similar questions of law pending before different High Courts to itself or to any one High Court.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 139A empowers the SC to consolidate cases raising common legal questions by transferring them — either to itself or to a single HC — to ensure uniform adjudication.

statement_analysis.statement: A transfer of cases under Article 139A can be initiated only on an application by a party to the case, and the Supreme Court has no power to act on its own motion.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 139A allows transfer on the SC's own motion, on application by the Attorney General of India, or on application by a party — the SC is not limited to party applications.

statement_analysis.statement: The transfer of a High Court judge under Article 222 is effected by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, and in practice, the Chief Justice's concurrence is effectively required after the Third Judges Case.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 222 requires Presidential consultation with the CJI; the Third Judges Case (1998) elevated this to effective concurrence as part of the collegium's primacy over judicial transfers.

solution.strong_distractor: d — A student who knows all three provisions broadly may assume all statements are correct without noticing the restriction in Statement 2 limiting transfers to party-initiated applications.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Art. 139A explicitly empowers SC to transfer to itself or to another HC — correct.
Statement 2: Art. 139A also allows SC's own motion and AG's application — not limited to party applications; incorrect.
Statement 3: Art. 222 read with Third Judges Case (1998) requires effective CJI concurrence — correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the conflation of 'party-initiated' with the full range of standing under Art. 139A. The provision specifically includes the Supreme Court's own motion and the Attorney General's application — two initiators students frequently overlook. This trap works because students who read Art. 139A quickly assume only aggrieved parties can move the SC, analogising to the normal adversarial model.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 139A and 222 deal with two categorically distinct transfers — one of cases, one of judges.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Art. 139A allows the SC to transfer cases involving common legal questions from multiple HCs to a single HC or to itself, ensuring legal uniformity.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The transfer can be initiated by the SC suo motu, by the Attorney General, or by any party to the case — not exclusively by parties.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Art. 222 transfers of HC judges require Presidential action with CJI consultation; post-Third Judges Case, the CJI's collegium recommendation is practically determinative.

Value Addition:
• Art. 139A is commonly used for matters of national constitutional importance (e.g., challenges to a central law filed in multiple HCs simultaneously).
• Art. 222 transfers are distinct from the appointment of additional judges under Art. 224.
• A judge transferred under Art. 222 is entitled to compensatory allowance as determined by Parliament.

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 130 — CJI designates SC seat with Presidential approval
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students familiar with Parliament's general role in constitutional matters may assume Parliament designates the SC's location, when in fact Art. 130 gives this power to the CJI with Presidential approval.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Parliament has no role in designating where the SC sits under Art. 130.
Eliminate (c): The President alone cannot unilaterally designate SC locations; Art. 130 requires CJI's initiative with Presidential approval.
Eliminate (d): The SC does not designate its own seat without Presidential approval.
Confirm (b): Article 130 provides that the SC sits in Delhi or such other place(s) as the CJI may, with the approval of the President, appoint.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students often assume that since Delhi is the established seat of the SC, the Constitution must have permanently fixed it. Article 130 deliberately avoids this — it gives the CJI discretionary power (with Presidential approval) to hold sittings elsewhere, which is the basis for the recurring demand for regional circuit benches. The trap is the assumption that permanence implies constitutional fixation.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 130 addresses the physical location of the Supreme Court's sittings, and it deliberately avoids permanently fixing Delhi as the sole seat.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Parliament has no constitutional authority over the SC's sitting locations under Art. 130.
• Option (b) — Correct: Article 130 specifies that the SC shall sit in Delhi or such other place(s) as the CJI may, with the President's approval, designate from time to time.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The President alone cannot make this determination; the CJI's initiative is the constitutionally required first step.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: While the SC has inherent powers, designating its own seat without Presidential approval is not within its constitutional authority.

Value Addition:
• The CJI's power under Art. 130 is the constitutional basis for demands to establish circuit benches in southern or northeastern India.
• Art. 145(3) requires a minimum 5-judge bench for substantial constitutional questions — this is distinct from the general quorum of 3.
• The general quorum for SC sittings is 3 judges, as prescribed under the Supreme Court Rules read with Art. 145(2).

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 32 suspension under Art. 359 — Arts. 20 and 21 not suspendable

statement_analysis.statement: Article 32 of the Constitution can be suspended during a National Emergency proclaimed under Article 352 by a Presidential order under Article 359.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 359 allows the President to suspend the right to move any court for enforcement of fundamental rights (other than Arts. 20 and 21) during a National Emergency — Art. 32 is suspendable to this extent.

statement_analysis.statement: Even during a National Emergency under Article 352, the rights guaranteed under Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended, and consequently, the right to approach the Supreme Court for their enforcement under Article 32 remains intact.
statement_analysis.reason: The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) inserted the proviso that Arts. 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even by a Presidential order under Art. 359; therefore, Art. 32 for enforcing these two rights remains available.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 226 of the Constitution, which empowers High Courts to issue writs, is also a Fundamental Right and can be suspended by a Presidential order during a National Emergency.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 226 is not a Fundamental Right — it is in Part VI (High Courts) of the Constitution. Only Art. 32 is a FR (Part III). Art. 226 cannot be suspended by a Presidential order under Art. 359.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know that Art. 226 is broader in scope than Art. 32 may confuse 'broader power' with 'higher constitutional status,' assuming Art. 226 is also a FR that can be suspended like Art. 32.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Art. 359 allows suspension of Art. 32 during National Emergency (except for Arts. 20 and 21 enforcement) — Statement 1 is correct, not an error.
Statement 2: 44th Amendment's proviso explicitly protects Arts. 20 and 21 from suspension, keeping Art. 32 alive for these rights — Statement 2 is correct, not an error.
Statement 3: Art. 226 is not a Fundamental Right; it cannot be suspended by Art. 359 orders; it sits in Part VI, not Part III — Statement 3 is incorrect.
Only Statement 3 is NOT correct — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 deploys the scope-extension trap by mischaracterising Art. 226 as a Fundamental Right. Students who know Art. 226 gives broader writ powers than Art. 32 may assume that 'broader' also means 'constitutional right of equal status.' The distinction is critical: Art. 32 is in Part III and is itself a FR; Art. 226 is in Part VI and is a judicial power, not a personal right. Accordingly, Art. 226 cannot be suspended by a Presidential proclamation under Art. 359.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between Art. 32 and Art. 226 in terms of constitutional status is fundamental. Article 32 is a Fundamental Right — the right to move the SC itself. Article 226 is a constitutional power of the HC, not a Fundamental Right.

• Statement 1 — Correct (not the error): Art. 32 can be suspended under Art. 359 during National Emergency, except for enforcement of Arts. 20 and 21.
• Statement 2 — Correct (not the error): The 44th Amendment (1978) entrenched Arts. 20 and 21 as unsuspendable, preserving Art. 32's availability for their enforcement.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect (the error): Art. 226 is a constitutional power, not a Fundamental Right. It resides in Part VI of the Constitution and cannot be suspended by Art. 359 orders, which only reach Fundamental Rights in Part III.

Value Addition:
• Dr. Ambedkar called Art. 32 the 'heart and soul of the Constitution' — a frequently quoted statement.
• Art. 226 is wider in subject matter (FRs + other legal rights) but lower in constitutional hierarchy (not a FR itself).
• Art. 359 suspension requires a Presidential Order specifying which FRs are suspended — it is not automatic on Emergency proclamation.

concepts_used: Ad Hoc Judges and Acting CJI Appointments

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 126, 127, 128 — Acting CJI, ad hoc, and retired judge distinctions

statement_analysis.statement: Article 127 empowers the Chief Justice of India to appoint an ad hoc judge from a High Court to sit in the Supreme Court when the Supreme Court lacks the quorum required for its sittings.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 127 explicitly provides for this — the CJI may do so with consent of the HC Chief Justice and after consultation with the President.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 128, a retired judge of the Supreme Court may be requested by the Chief Justice of India (with prior consent of the President) to sit and act as a Supreme Court judge.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 128 creates this mechanism specifically for retired SC judges — distinct from ad hoc judges under Art. 127 who are drawn from High Courts.

statement_analysis.statement: When the office of the Chief Justice of India is vacant, the next senior-most judge of the Supreme Court automatically assumes the role of Chief Justice by operation of Article 126.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 126 vests the power of appointment of an Acting CJI in the President — the next senior judge does not automatically assume the role; a Presidential appointment is constitutionally required.

statement_analysis.statement: An ad hoc judge appointed under Article 127 has the same jurisdiction and powers as a regular judge of the Supreme Court during the period of such appointment.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 127(3) provides that an ad hoc judge while sitting shall have all the jurisdiction, powers, and privileges of a regular SC judge.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know seniority convention governs CJI appointment in practice may extend this to the vacancy scenario, assuming the next senior judge 'automatically' assumes acting charge — confusing convention with the Art. 126 presidential appointment requirement.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Art. 127 for quorum maintenance using HC judges — correct.
Statement 2: Art. 128 for retired SC judges — correct.
Statement 3: Art. 126 requires Presidential appointment of Acting CJI; no automatic succession — incorrect.
Statement 4: Art. 127(3) explicitly grants full jurisdiction to ad hoc judges — correct.
Three statements (1, 2, 4) are correct — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the entity-swap trap — students swap 'Presidential appointment' with 'automatic seniority-based succession.' In practice, the most senior available judge has always been appointed, but the constitutional text in Art. 126 requires a Presidential appointment, not automatic assumption. This distinction between convention and constitutional text is a recurring UPSC pattern.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 126, 127, and 128 create three separate mechanisms for staffing the SC when the regular complement is insufficient.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Art. 127 allows ad hoc judges from HCs when the SC quorum cannot be maintained, with consent of HC's CJ and Presidential consultation.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Art. 128 allows retired SC judges to be requested back; distinct from Art. 127 which draws from HCs.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Art. 126 requires a Presidential appointment for Acting CJI — the most senior judge does not automatically assume the role, even though convention has always followed seniority.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Art. 127(3) grants full SC jurisdiction to ad hoc judges during their tenure.

Three statements are correct — option (c).

Value Addition:
• Art. 127 (ad hoc from HC) and Art. 128 (retired SC judges) are both initiated by the CJI.
• The President's role in all three provisions (126, 127, 128) highlights executive involvement in SC functioning.
• Ad hoc judges under Art. 127 cannot be called if they have retired from the HC.

meta.subject: Polity
concepts_used: Doctrine of Judicial Review: Constitutional Basis and Scope

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 13 — primary textual basis for judicial review of legislation
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion correct? Yes: The doctrine of judicial review is not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution but is derived from multiple articles including Art. 13, 32, 131–136, 143, 226, and 227.

Step 2 — Is Reason correct? No: Article 13 declares that laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void — this IS the primary textual basis for judicial review of legislation. Saying Art. 13 'does not provide' textual basis is factually incorrect.
Step 3 — Since R is incorrect, the correct option must be (c): A is correct but R is incorrect.
Confirm: A is correct (judicial review not explicitly stated); R is incorrect (Art. 13 IS the primary textual basis); option (c) is the answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question traps students who accept R because of its authoritative-sounding phrasing. The Assertion is correct — 'judicial review' as a term does not appear in the Constitution. But the Reason incorrectly denies Art. 13 its role as the primary textual foundation. Students who agree with A and also know Art. 13 deals with laws inconsistent with FRs may still fail to notice R's denial of Art. 13's role, especially if they read quickly.
solution.final_explanation:
Judicial review is among the most powerful doctrines of Indian constitutional law, despite not being named anywhere in the constitutional text.

A — Correct: The phrase 'judicial review' does not appear in the Constitution; the doctrine is constructed from multiple provisions — Art. 13 (laws inconsistent with FRs are void), Art. 32 and 226 (writ jurisdiction), Arts. 131–136 (appellate routes), and Art. 143.
R — Incorrect: Article 13 explicitly states that any law inconsistent with or in derogation of Fundamental Rights shall be void. This is precisely the primary textual basis for judicial review of legislation. The claim that Art. 13 'does not provide explicit textual basis' is factually wrong.

Since A is correct but R is incorrect — option (c).

Value Addition:
• Post-Kesavananda Bharati (1973), even constitutional amendments are subject to judicial review if they violate basic structure.
• India's judicial review is broader than USA's in one sense — it extends to constitutional amendments.
• The doctrine of non-justiciability (political question doctrine) limits judicial review on certain executive/legislative decisions.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

Reason (R): Article 13 of the Constitution does not provide any explicit textual basis for judicial review of legislation; it only deals with the relationship between laws and Fundamental Rights in a general declaratory sense.

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect
(d) A is incorrect but R is correct

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 142 — complete justice power unique to SC; no HC equivalent
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know High Courts can issue directions under Art. 226 for 'any purpose' may assume this extends to the kind of 'complete justice' orders Art. 142 authorises, confusing the broader subject-matter scope of Art. 226 with Art. 142's special power.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Art. 142 does not confer legislative power on the SC; it allows orders to do complete justice within existing disputes, not to create new law permanently.
Confirm (b): Art. 142's power to pass any decree or order necessary for complete justice is unique to the SC — no equivalent exists for HCs.
Eliminate (c): Art. 226 gives HCs wider writ jurisdiction but does NOT include the 'complete justice' power under Art. 142; this power has no HC equivalent.
Eliminate (d): Art. 142 is not a writ provision; it is a separate, residual power to ensure complete justice in pending matters.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in option (c) conflates Art. 226's broader subject-matter jurisdiction with Art. 142's extraordinary complete-justice power. Many students, knowing Art. 226 is 'wider' than Art. 32, extrapolate this to assume HCs have an equivalent of Art. 142. In reality, Art. 142 is exclusively a Supreme Court power with no High Court parallel — a critically distinctive feature of SC jurisdiction.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 142 is one of the most uniquely powerful and exclusively Supreme Court-specific provisions in the Constitution.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Art. 142 does not make the SC a legislative body. Orders under it are passed to complete justice in specific pending cases, not to create permanent law.
• Option (b) — Correct: The power under Art. 142 to pass any decree or order necessary for complete justice in any pending matter is conferred exclusively on the Supreme Court. No equivalent exists for High Courts.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Art. 226 empowers HCs to issue writs for 'any other purpose' (beyond FRs), but this is different from Art. 142's extraordinary complete-justice jurisdiction, which HCs do not possess.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Art. 142 is not a writ-issuing provision; it is a residual power to pass any order needed to do complete justice.

Value Addition:
• Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) is a landmark use of Art. 142 — SC issued binding guidelines in the legislative vacuum on sexual harassment.
• Vineet Narain (1998) is another case where Art. 142 was used to direct CBI investigation independently.
• Art. 142 is sometimes critiqued as enabling 'judicial legislation' — a core tension in judicial activism debates.

(b) It confers upon the Supreme Court the unique power to pass any decree or order necessary to do complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it — a power that has no equivalent in the jurisdiction of High Courts
(c) It empowers the High Courts, like the Supreme Court, to issue orders for complete justice in any pending matter involving Fundamental Rights under Article 226
(d) It is a writ-issuing power that supplements the Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Article 32 in matters not involving Fundamental Rights

concepts_used: Inter-State Water Disputes and Exclusion from SC's Original Jurisdiction
Original Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (Art. 131)

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 262 exclusion of SC — tribunal award has force of SC decree

statement_analysis.statement: Article 262 empowers Parliament to exclude the Supreme Court's jurisdiction over inter-state water disputes, and such an exclusion has been effected through the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 262 explicitly gives Parliament this power, and the 1956 Act has exercised it — the SC cannot be approached directly for such disputes once a tribunal is constituted.

statement_analysis.statement: An award given by a tribunal constituted under the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956 has the same legal force as a decree of the Supreme Court of India.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act provides that once an award is published by the Central Government, it has the same force and effect as an order or decree of the SC — making it final and binding.

statement_analysis.statement: Since inter-state water disputes are excluded from Article 131's scope, the Supreme Court has no role whatsoever in matters involving inter-state rivers or river valleys after a tribunal is constituted.
statement_analysis.reason: The exclusion bars direct invocation of Art. 131 for the water dispute itself, but the SC retains jurisdiction over related constitutional questions, contempt, and enforcement — 'no role whatsoever' is an overbroad statement.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know both Statements 1 and 2 are correct may assume Statement 3 is also correct, having heard that 'SC has no jurisdiction over water disputes' as a general rule and extending it to all matters touching inter-state rivers.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Art. 262 empowerment and 1956 Act exclusion are well-established — correct.
Statement 2: The award's equivalence to an SC decree is a specific statutory provision of the 1956 Act — correct.
Statement 3: 'No role whatsoever' overstates the exclusion; the SC retains jurisdiction over constitutional questions and enforcement matters even after a tribunal is set up — incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 deploys the scope-extension trap using 'whatsoever' — a single word that converts a partial truth into a false absolute. The SC's exclusion from inter-state water disputes is specific to the water dispute itself under Art. 131; the SC retains powers over related constitutional questions. Students who generalise the exclusion to 'any matter touching inter-state rivers' will accept Statement 3 as correct and choose an incorrect option.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 262 is the constitutional exception that carves inter-state water disputes out of the SC's ordinary federal jurisdiction under Art. 131.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Art. 262 explicitly empowers Parliament to bar SC jurisdiction; the Inter-State Water Disputes Act 1956 has done so.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Once published by the Central Government, tribunal awards under the 1956 Act have the same force as SC decrees — making them practically equivalent to final judicial orders.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The exclusion applies to the water dispute proper; the SC retains ancillary jurisdiction on constitutional questions and enforcement. 'No role whatsoever' is an impermissible absolute.

Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option (a).

Value Addition:
• The Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal, Ravi and Beas Waters Tribunal are examples of such bodies.
• Despite the exclusion, the SC has in practice examined procedural aspects of tribunal proceedings.
• Art. 262 is the only constitutional provision that explicitly allows Parliament to exclude the SC's jurisdiction — a significant exception to judicial supremacy.

Appointment of CJI and the Collegium System

solution.concept_anchor: Distinguished jurist route — never used; collegium primacy for SC appointments
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the President plays a formal role in judicial appointments may assume Presidential discretion is the operative principle when the collegium has not recommended a name, without knowing that the collegium's primacy under the Second and Third Judges Cases effectively governs.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The NJAC was struck down in 2015; there is no functional NJAC to make this recommendation.
Eliminate (b): Presidential discretion is constrained by the collegium system post-Second Judges Case; the President cannot unilaterally appoint without collegium recommendation.
Confirm (c): The collegium (CJI + 4 senior-most judges) must evaluate and recommend even the distinguished jurist route — the route's constitutionality does not bypass collegium primacy.
Eliminate (d): Parliament has no role in individual SC appointments; Parliament only legislates on the total number of judges.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) plants a 'plausible-fabrication' trap — the NJAC sounds authoritative and was indeed a recent constitutional development, but it was struck down in 2015 and has no operative existence. Students who remember '99th Amendment' and 'NJAC' as connected may select (a) thinking the NJAC remains functional for unusual appointments like the distinguished jurist route.
solution.final_explanation:
The 'distinguished jurist' route under Art. 124(3)(c) is constitutionally valid but has never been used in India. A scenario raising it tests both the qualification provisions and the collegium appointment mechanism.

Applicable principle: Even for the distinguished jurist route, the appointment must flow through the collegium process (CJI + 4 senior-most judges), as established by the Third Judges Case (1998). The President's opinion about a person's distinction as a jurist feeds into the collegium's deliberation — it does not create an independent Presidential appointment channel.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The NJAC (99th Amendment) was declared unconstitutional in October 2015 and has no operative existence.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Presidential discretion is constrained by the collegium system; the President acts on the collegium's recommendation, not independently.
• Option (c) — Correct: The collegium must recommend even for distinguished jurist appointments; Presidential opinion on 'distinction' is an eligibility input, not a bypass of the collegium process.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Parliament's role is limited to prescribing the number of judges by legislation — it has no role in individual appointments.

Value Addition:
• Despite being constitutionally available since 1950, the distinguished jurist route has never been used in India.
• The UK's legal system (and previously, the US) have equivalent routes that are actively used.
• 'Distinguished jurist' is assessed subjectively by the President, making it the most flexible — and most politically sensitive — of the three eligibility routes.

solution.concept_anchor: Constitutional, civil, criminal appellate provisions — Art. 132–134
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students often confuse Art. 132 (constitutional appeals) with Art. 133 (civil appeals) since both require a 'substantial question of law' certificate, making the A entry in option (a) look plausible.
elimination_logic: A: Art. 132 covers any HC judgment (civil, criminal, or other) involving a substantial question as to constitutional interpretation — matches with '3'.

B: Art. 133 governs civil appeals where HC certifies a substantial question of general legal importance — the value-of-subject-matter requirement was removed by 30th Amendment (1972) — matches with '1'.
C: Art. 134 grants appeal as of right to SC in criminal matters where HC reverses acquittal to death sentence — matches with '4'.
D: Art. 32 is not an appellate provision; it is the original FR-enforcement jurisdiction of the SC, itself a Fundamental Right — matches with '2'.
Correct: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in this match-the-column is the A/B entity swap — Art. 132 and Art. 133 both involve 'substantial question of law' certificates, and students frequently interchangeably apply this phrase to both without distinguishing that Art. 132 is limited to constitutional interpretation questions while Art. 133 is for general civil law questions of public importance. The 30th Amendment detail (removal of value requirement for civil appeals) further tests precision.
solution.final_explanation:
The SC's appellate jurisdiction spans three distinct constitutional routes, each with specific preconditions.

Correct pairings:
• A — Article 132 (List entry 3): Appeals from any HC judgment on substantial questions of constitutional interpretation — applies to civil, criminal, or other proceedings.
• B — Article 133 (List entry 1): Civil appeals; the 30th Amendment (1972) removed the value-of-subject-matter requirement, making certificate from HC based on substantial general legal importance the sole criterion.
• C — Article 134 (List entry 4): Criminal appeals as of right when HC reverses acquittal and imposes death sentence; other criminal appeals require a certificate.
• D — Article 32 (List entry 2): Not an appellate provision — it is the original FR enforcement jurisdiction, itself a Fundamental Right under Part III.

The primary trap is the A-B swap: both Art. 132 and Art. 133 involve 'substantial question of law' but of categorically different types.

Value Addition:
• Art. 136 SLP is the residual appellate route covering all gaps left by Arts. 132–135.
• Art. 132 is the only appellate provision that cuts across civil, criminal, and other cases.
• Art. 134A (added by 44th Amendment) requires HCs to give certificates on appeal to SC in Art. 132/133/134 matters.

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 136 SLP — exceptions, discretionary nature, interlocutory orders

statement_analysis.statement: An SLP under Article 136 can be filed against interlocutory orders passed by a High Court, in addition to final judgments and decrees.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 136 covers 'any judgment, decree, determination, sentence or order' — this broad language includes interlocutory orders, and the SC has entertained SLPs against interlocutory orders in appropriate cases.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 136 expressly excludes the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court over judgments passed by courts martial or military tribunals.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 136(2) is an express constitutional bar — the SC cannot entertain SLPs from Armed Forces Tribunal or court martial proceedings.

statement_analysis.statement: Once a party files an SLP and the Supreme Court admits it, the petitioner has an absolute right to have the case finally decided on merits, and the Court cannot dismiss it at the stage of hearing without assigning reasons.
statement_analysis.reason: SLP is discretionary at every stage; even after admission, the SC may dismiss at the hearing stage and has the power to refuse without giving reasons — there is no absolute right to a merits decision.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that admission of an SLP is different from filing may assume that 'admission' creates an enforceable right to merits adjudication, making Statement 3 appear correct and pointing away from (c).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Art. 136's language ('any... order') includes interlocutory orders — correct; not an error.
Statement 2: Art. 136(2) expressly excludes military tribunal orders — correct; not an error.
Statement 3: SLP is purely discretionary — no absolute right exists even post-admission; the SC retains power to dismiss summarily at any stage — incorrect.
Only Statement 3 is NOT correct — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the procedural misunderstanding about what 'admission' of an SLP means. Students often assume that once the SC admits (grants leave for) an SLP, the matter must proceed to full merits adjudication. In reality, Art. 136 is described by the SC itself as a discretionary, extraordinary jurisdiction that the Court exercises with restraint — even post-admission, matters can be disposed of summarily. The 'absolute right' language is the scope-extension element that makes Statement 3 incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 136 is the SC's residual appellate power, defined by its extraordinary discretionary character.

• Statement 1 — Correct (not the error): The word 'order' in Art. 136 is broad enough to cover interlocutory orders; the SC has repeatedly admitted SLPs against interim directions of HCs.
• Statement 2 — Correct (not the error): Art. 136(2) is an express exclusion — courts-martial and armed forces tribunals are outside SLP jurisdiction.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect (the error): SLP remains discretionary throughout. Admission does not create an absolute right to merits adjudication; the SC can and does dismiss admitted matters summarily in appropriate cases without detailed reasons.

Value Addition:
• The distinction between 'filing' an SLP and 'granting leave' (admission) is procedurally important — many SLPs are dismissed in limine.
• Once leave is granted and SLP converts into a regular appeal, it follows a different procedural track with oral arguments.
• Art. 136 is also available against orders of quasi-judicial bodies and statutory tribunals, not just courts.

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 143 advisory opinion — non-binding; distinct from Art. 141 precedent

statement_analysis.statement: An opinion rendered by the Supreme Court under Article 143 is not binding on the President and does not constitute a precedent under Article 141 for other courts.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 143 opinions are advisory — the President is not obligated to follow them, and they are not 'law declared by the SC' in the sense of Art. 141 since they are not decisions in adversarial proceedings.

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike the United States Supreme Court, the Supreme Court of India possesses advisory jurisdiction under Article 143, meaning it can render opinions on questions of law or fact of public importance referred by the President.
statement_analysis.reason: The USA's Supreme Court has consistently declined to render advisory opinions and has no such constitutional provision; India's Art. 143 is a distinctive feature of the Indian constitutional design.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know that advisory opinions are 'merely advisory' may assume they have zero precedential value in all circumstances, leading them to accept Statement 1 as correct while wrongly doubting Statement 2's comparative claim about the USA.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Advisory opinions under Art. 143 are not binding on the President and not precedents under Art. 141 — this is settled constitutional law; Statement 1 is correct.

Statement 2: The USA Supreme Court has no advisory jurisdiction — this is a well-known comparative constitutional law fact; the Indian SC's Art. 143 power is unique among common law apex courts; Statement 2 is correct.
Both statements are correct — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap here lies in blending Art. 143 advisory opinions with Art. 141 precedents. Students who know the SC is the supreme court of law and its pronouncements are binding may wrongly extend this to advisory opinions. The distinction is that Art. 141's binding nature applies to judicial decisions in contested proceedings — advisory opinions under Art. 143 operate in a structurally different mode and are categorically non-binding.
solution.final_explanation:
The advisory jurisdiction under Art. 143 and the precedent-creating jurisdiction under Art. 141 are constitutionally distinct tracks of the Supreme Court's authority.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The SC's advisory opinion is not binding on the President, who may or may not accept it. It also does not qualify as 'law declared by the Supreme Court' under Art. 141 since it is not a decision in adversarial litigation.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The US Supreme Court has categorically refused to render advisory opinions since the Washington Administration era; India's Art. 143 is a meaningful point of distinction in comparative constitutional design.

Both statements are correct — option (a).

Value Addition:
• The SC may decline to answer references under the first category of Art. 143 (as it did in the 1993 Ayodhya reference).
• Pre-Constitution treaty references fall under the mandatory second category — the SC cannot decline.
• Despite being non-binding, advisory opinions carry significant persuasive weight and often influence subsequent judicial decisions.

solution.concept_anchor: Review → Curative petition sequence; Contempt Act 2006 amendment
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know the Contempt of Courts Act was passed in 1971 and the Rupa Ashok Hurra case was in 2002 may not know when the truth-defence amendment came, potentially placing IV before III.
elimination_logic: Contempt of Courts Act 1971 enacted — this is first (I) as the baseline statutory framework.
Rupa Ashok Hurra case 2002 — established the Curative Petition doctrine; this is second (II).
Truth as a defence amendment to the Contempt of Courts Act — this came in 2006, after the Rupa Ashok Hurra case; third (III).
NJAC struck down (Fourth Judges Case / NJAC case) — October 2015; fourth (IV).
Correct order: I → II → III → IV — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The primary temporal trap is between II (Rupa Ashok Hurra, 2002) and III (truth defence amendment, 2006). Students who know both events are post-2000 may invert their order, placing the 2006 amendment before the 2002 case. Additionally, students who conflate the original Contempt of Courts Act's passage (1971) with subsequent amendments may misplace event I.
solution.final_explanation:
These four events trace the evolution of SC's self-correcting mechanisms and independence safeguards.

Correct sequence:
I. Contempt of Courts Act enacted (1971): Codified the law of contempt while preserving the SC's inherent contempt power under Art. 129.
II. Rupa Ashok Hurra case (2002): Judicially created the Curative Petition — the last post-review remedy available before an SC order becomes absolutely final.
III. 2006 Amendment to Contempt of Courts Act: Inserted 'truth' as a valid defence in contempt proceedings — significant liberalisation of contempt law.
IV. NJAC struck down (2015): SC upheld judicial independence by invalidating the 99th Constitutional Amendment — judicial primacy in appointments reaffirmed.

Why other orders fail: Placing III before II ignores that the truth-defence amendment postdates the Rupa Ashok Hurra case by four years.

Value Addition:
• The truth defence (2006) was inserted following academic criticism that truth-telling could constitute contempt.
• Curative Petitions are entertained by SC only in rarest cases involving denial of natural justice.
• The NJAC case (2015) is sometimes called the 'Fourth Judges Case' in academic literature.

solution.concept_anchor: Second Judges Case — 'consultation' elevated to 'concurrence'
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the collegium exists and the Third Judges Case refined it may attribute the shift from 'consultation' to 'concurrence' to the Third (1998) rather than the Second Judges Case (1993).
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The First Judges Case (1981) held that Presidential consultation with the CJI was not binding — it did the opposite of establishing concurrence.
Eliminate (b): The Third Judges Case (1998) settled the composition of the collegium and expanded it to CJI + 4 judges — it did not originally create the 'concurrence' requirement.
Eliminate (c): The NJAC case (2015) struck down the 99th Amendment — this came after concurrence was already established.
Confirm (d): The Second Judges Case (1993) is where the SC elevated 'consultation' to mean effective 'concurrence,' establishing the primacy of the CJI and the collegium in appointments.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The three Judges Cases are among the most tested events in UPSC Prelims on the judiciary. The entity-swap trap between Second (1993) and Third (1998) Judges Cases is extremely common because both involve the collegium. Students who recall '1998 = collegium primacy' without being precise about which case established what will choose option (b). The Second Judges Case established primacy; the Third Judges Case refined the collegium's composition and process.
solution.final_explanation:
The evolution of the collegium system passed through three landmark rulings, each shifting the balance of appointment power further toward the judiciary.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The First Judges Case (1981) held that 'consultation' was not binding on the President — it actually weakened judicial primacy at that point.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Third Judges Case (1998) defined the collegium's composition (CJI + 4 senior-most judges) and procedures, but the transformation of 'consultation' to 'concurrence' was the Second Judges Case.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The NJAC case (2015) struck down the 99th Amendment — it came 22 years after concurrence was established.
• Option (d) — Correct: The Second Judges Case (1993) — S.C. Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India — reinterpreted 'consultation' under Art. 124 to mean effective concurrence of the CJI, establishing collegium primacy.

Value Addition:
• All three Judges Cases involved Art. 124's 'consultation' language.
• The Second Judges Case overruled the First Judges Case on the binding nature of CJI's advice.
• Post-Second Judges Case, the President can return a recommendation but must accept if the collegium reiterates it.

solution.concept_anchor: Judicial independence safeguards — security of tenure, salary, prohibition on discussion
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may identify option (b) as odd because it involves post-retirement conduct, making it feel distinctly different from in-service protections, when in fact it is a genuine constitutional independence safeguard.
elimination_logic: Identify the common feature: Options (a), (b), and (d) are direct constitutional mechanisms to insulate serving and retired judges from political pressure — all are genuine independence safeguards.

Evaluate (c): The President appointing the Acting CJI when the CJI post is vacant (Art. 126) is an administrative/structural provision — it deals with continuity of the institution, not the independence of individual judges. No independence-safeguard function is served by this provision.
Option (c) is the odd one out — it belongs to the category of institutional continuity, not judicial independence safeguards.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) (retired judges barred from SC practice) is the deliberate attractive distractor. Students who see 'post-retirement restriction' and compare it to the active-service provisions in (a) and (d) may classify (b) as structurally different. However, Art. 124(7)'s bar on post-retirement practice before the SC is precisely an independence safeguard — it prevents a retiring judge from compromising impartiality to cultivate future clients. The true odd one out is (c), which is an administrative continuity provision.
solution.final_explanation:
Judicial independence is protected through multiple safeguards — some apply during service, some after retirement, and some protect judges from legislative scrutiny.

• Option (a) — Shares the common feature: Salaries of SC judges charged to the Consolidated Fund (Art. 125) insulate them from Parliamentary pressure on pay — a direct independence safeguard.
• Option (b) — Shares the common feature: Art. 124(7)'s bar on retired SC judges practising before the SC prevents compromising impartiality for future professional gain — an independence safeguard.
• Option (c) — Does NOT share: Art. 126's provision for Presidential appointment of an Acting CJI when the post falls vacant is an institutional continuity provision, not a judicial independence mechanism. It does not protect any individual judge's independence.
• Option (d) — Shares the common feature: Art. 121's prohibition on legislative discussion of judges' conduct (except on removal) insulates judges from parliamentary criticism — a clear independence safeguard.

Value Addition:
• Art. 124(7) applies only to the SC, not HCs — a frequently missed precision.
• Judges' salaries cannot be reduced to their disadvantage after appointment (Art. 125(2)).
• The charged-expenditure status of judicial salaries means Parliament cannot withhold them through the budget process.
