solution.concept_anchor: Art. 131 exclusions — private parties, pre-Constitution treaties, Art. 262 water disputes

statement_analysis.statement: Article 131 does not extend to disputes in which a private party is one of the disputants, even if the dispute involves a question of constitutional law affecting Centre-State relations.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 131 is limited to disputes between the Centre and States or between States — the moment a private party is involved, Art. 131 jurisdiction is excluded.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 131's jurisdiction extends to all inter-State disputes, including those relating to sharing of river waters between two or more States.
statement_analysis.reason: Inter-state water disputes are specifically excluded from Art. 131 by Art. 262, which empowers Parliament to bar SC jurisdiction — such disputes go to statutory tribunals under the Inter-State Water Disputes Act 1956.

statement_analysis.statement: Both Article 32 and Article 131 confer original jurisdiction on the Supreme Court, but they differ in the nature of the right being enforced — Article 32 is for Fundamental Rights enforcement while Article 131 is for federal dispute resolution.
statement_analysis.reason: This distinction is constitutionally accurate — Art. 32 is triggered by FR violations (private or government parties can invoke it) while Art. 131 is limited to Centre-State or State-State governmental disputes of a federal character.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know Art. 131 gives 'exclusive' original jurisdiction may assume that 'exclusive and original' means it covers all inter-state matters including water disputes, leading them to mark Statement 2 as correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Art. 131's text limits parties to Centre and States — private parties excluded; correct.
Statement 2: Art. 262 and 1956 Act create a specific exclusion for water disputes from Art. 131 — Statement 2's claim of full coverage is wrong; incorrect.
Statement 3: The Art. 32 vs. Art. 131 distinction is well-established — both original, different purposes; correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a scope-extension tactic — the word 'all' inter-state disputes makes a facially plausible claim that fails because water disputes are carved out by Art. 262. Students who conflate 'inter-state dispute' with 'Art. 131 dispute' without recalling the Art. 262 exception will mark Statement 2 as correct. This is a consistently tested exclusion in UPSC questions on SC jurisdiction.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 131's 'exclusive original jurisdiction' is exclusive but not unlimited — it is bounded by specific exclusions that the Constitution and Parliament have created.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Art. 131 is restricted to government-to-government disputes (Centre-State or State-State). If a private party is involved, the appropriate remedy shifts to Art. 32 or HC writs or ordinary courts.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The word 'all' makes this false. Water disputes between states fall outside Art. 131 because Art. 262 empowers Parliament to exclude SC jurisdiction, and the 1956 Act has done so.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Both Art. 32 and Art. 131 are original jurisdiction provisions, but their triggers are entirely different — FR enforcement vs. federal governmental disputes.

Value Addition:
• Disputes arising under pre-Constitution treaties are also excluded from Art. 131.
• Art. 131 exclusivity means HCs cannot adjudicate genuine Centre-State constitutional disputes.
• Despite Art. 131's exclusivity, the SC can grant leave under Art. 136 in related matters that do not qualify under Art. 131 strictly.

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 142 complete justice — judicial activism vs. overreach distinction
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion correct? Yes: Article 142 empowers the SC to pass any decree or order necessary for complete justice; the Vishaka case (1997) and Vineet Narain (1998) are landmark uses of this power to fill legislative vacuums.

Step 2 — Is Reason correct? Yes: India follows functional (not strict) separation of powers; the SC can issue directions to the executive under Arts. 32 and 142 precisely because strict separation is not followed — the Constitution distributes powers with checks rather than rigid walls.

Step 3 — Does R explain A? Yes: The SC's ability to issue binding directions to the executive under Art. 142 (A) is causally grounded in India's functional — rather than strict — separation of powers model (R), which permits inter-branch judicial direction in the interest of justice.
Both A and R correct and R explains A — correct option is (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 142 and India's model of separation of powers are deeply interconnected. The SC's ability to issue 'complete justice' directions to the executive is only possible because India does not follow strict separation.

A — Correct: Art. 142's complete-justice power has been used to fill legislative and executive gaps — Vishaka (sexual harassment guidelines), Vineet Narain (CBI investigation directions), and T.N. Godavarman (forest governance directions) are landmark examples.
R — Correct: India's Constitution follows functional separation of powers with checks and balances rather than strict separation. Articles 32 and 142 explicitly authorise the SC to direct executive action — impossible under a strict separation model.
Causal connection: India's functional separation of powers (R) is the structural reason why Art. 142 can empower the SC to issue directions to the executive without violating constitutional limits (A). R directly explains why A is constitutionally valid.

Value Addition:
• Judicial activism refers to filling legislative vacuum; judicial overreach refers to encroaching on policy-making — a nuanced distinction tested in Mains.
• Art. 142 has no HC equivalent — reinforcing SC's unique constitutional position.
• The political question doctrine limits judicial review even under Art. 142 — courts will not substitute their judgment for executive policy choices.

solution.concept_anchor: Constitutional bench strength, quorum, and SC seat provisions

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 145(3), any case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution must be heard by a bench of not less than five judges.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 145(3) is explicit — the minimum bench strength for constitutional interpretation questions is five judges, commonly called the Constitution Bench.

statement_analysis.statement: The minimum quorum for a sitting of the Supreme Court is five judges, as prescribed under Article 145(3).
statement_analysis.reason: Article 145(3) sets the minimum for constitutional matters at five judges; the general quorum for ordinary SC sittings is three judges under the Supreme Court Rules read with Art. 145(2) — the two requirements are different.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 130 provides that the Supreme Court shall sit only in New Delhi, and any sitting in another location would require a constitutional amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 130 provides that the SC shall sit in Delhi OR such other place(s) as the CJI may appoint with Presidential approval — New Delhi is not permanently fixed and no constitutional amendment is needed for alternate sittings.

statement_analysis.statement: The right under Article 32 to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights is itself a Fundamental Right and is placed in Part III of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 32 is located in Part III and the right to constitutional remedies — including the right to approach the SC — is guaranteed as a Fundamental Right, not merely a procedural remedy.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who confuse constitutional bench strength (5) with general quorum (3) will mark Statement 2 as correct and potentially reach 'Only three' — making option (c) an attractive but incorrect choice for them.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Art. 145(3) minimum 5 judges for constitutional questions — correct.
Statement 2: General quorum is 3 (not 5); the 5-judge requirement is only for constitutional questions — incorrect.
Statement 3: Art. 130 does not permanently fix Delhi; CJI + Presidential approval can designate other locations — incorrect.
Statement 4: Art. 32 in Part III = FR status — correct.
Two statements (1 and 4) are correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the scope-extension trap by applying the 5-judge constitutional bench requirement universally to all SC sittings. The UPSC has repeatedly tested the distinction between the general quorum (3 judges) and the constitutional bench minimum (5 judges). Students who recall '5 judges' in the context of SC sittings often misapply it as the general quorum, leading them to mark Statement 2 correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Two distinct numerical thresholds apply to SC sittings, and conflating them is a classic UPSC trap.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Art. 145(3) requires a minimum 5-judge Constitution Bench for substantial constitutional interpretation questions.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The general quorum for SC sittings is 3 judges (prescribed under the Supreme Court Rules), not 5. The 5-judge requirement is specific to constitutional questions only.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Art. 130 does not permanently fix Delhi as the exclusive seat. The CJI, with Presidential approval, can designate other venues — no amendment required.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Art. 32 is in Part III and is itself a Fundamental Right — this is why Dr. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul of the Constitution.'

Statements 1 and 4 are correct — option (b).

Value Addition:
• Constitutional Benches decide matters of constitutional importance; Division Benches (typically 2-3 judges) handle most regular appeals.
• Art. 145(2) requires at least 3 judges to declare any central law invalid — distinct from Art. 145(3).
• PIL petitions under Art. 32 are typically heard by Division Benches of 2–3 judges.

solution.concept_anchor: 30th Amendment removed value-of-subject-matter from Art. 133
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may accept option (a) as correct because they know Art. 134 deals with criminal appeals — the 'reversed acquittal' formulation sounds right without recalling the specific sentence threshold (death sentence, not merely any imprisonment).
elimination_logic: Evaluate (a): Art. 134 gives appeal as of right when HC reverses acquittal to death sentence — the pairing says 'reversal of acquittal to imprisonment for any period,' which omits the death-sentence or 10-year thresholds; incorrectly matched.

Evaluate (b): The 44th Amendment (1978) inserted protection for Arts. 20 and 21; the 30th Amendment (1972) removed the value requirement from Art. 133 civil appeals — option (b) swaps these; incorrectly matched.
Evaluate (c): Art. 136(2) explicitly bars SLP from military tribunal orders — this pairing is correct.
Evaluate (d): The 'distinguished jurist' route is Art. 124(3)(c), not Art. 124(3)(b) which is the Bar advocate route — incorrectly matched.
Option (c) is correctly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is the primary trap — students who know Art. 134 involves criminal appeals and reversed acquittals may accept the broad formulation 'reversal to any imprisonment' without recalling that the right of appeal as of right requires either a death sentence or 10+ years imprisonment. The temporal-swap trap in option (b) swaps the 30th and 44th Amendments — both are post-1970 and students who remember 'an amendment changed Art. 133' often mix up which amendment number.
solution.final_explanation:
Precision on both the provisions and amendment numbers is critical for appellate jurisdiction questions.

• Option (a) — Incorrectly matched: Art. 134 gives criminal appeal as of right only when HC reverses acquittal to the death sentence, or certifies the case. 'Any period of imprisonment' is too broad — both the death-sentence threshold and the 10+ year threshold are specific requirements.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: The amendment that removed the monetary value requirement from Art. 133 civil appeals was the 30th Amendment (1972), not the 44th Amendment (1978). The 44th Amendment protected Arts. 20 and 21 from suspension.
• Option (c) — Correctly matched: Art. 136(2) explicitly states that SLP shall not apply to any judgment or order passed by any court or tribunal constituted by or under any law relating to the Armed Forces. This is the express constitutional bar.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: The 'distinguished jurist' route is Art. 124(3)(c), not (3)(b). Art. 124(3)(b) is the High Court advocate route requiring 10 years of Bar practice.

Value Addition:
• Art. 136(2)'s exclusion of armed forces is one of only two express exclusions in Art. 136 — the other being the narrow requirement of 'court or tribunal in India.'
• The 30th Amendment (1972) was passed specifically to reduce backlog in SC civil appeals by removing the rupee-value threshold.
• Art. 124(3)(c)'s distinguished jurist route remains constitutionally alive but practically unused.

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 139A case transfer — own motion, AG, or party application
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the SC can transfer cases may attribute this power to Art. 142 (complete justice) rather than Art. 139A (case transfer), confusing the general extraordinary power with the specific transfer provision.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Art. 142 is a complete-justice power for pending SC matters — it does not govern the transfer of cases between HCs or from HCs to the SC; that is Art. 139A.

Confirm (b): Art. 139A allows the SC to transfer cases raising common substantial questions of law from one HC to another or to itself — applicable when multiple HCs are deciding the same constitutional question differently.
Eliminate (c): Art. 131 is the Centre-State original jurisdiction — it does not apply to constitutional challenge cases filed by private parties in HCs.
Eliminate (d): Art. 136 SLP is a post-decision remedy for appellate review — the scenario describes a pre-decision transfer of pending cases, not an appeal from a decided case.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is the conflation trap: students who know Art. 142 is the SC's extraordinary power may apply it here, not distinguishing that Art. 142 applies to cases already before the SC while Art. 139A is the specific provision for transferring cases from HCs. The distinction between these two powers is functionally significant — Art. 139A avoids contradictory HC decisions; Art. 142 ensures complete justice in SC matters.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 139A is a specialised transfer jurisdiction that prevents legal fragmentation when the same constitutional question is litigated simultaneously before multiple High Courts.

Applicable principle: Art. 139A empowers the SC to transfer cases involving the same or substantially similar questions of law pending before any HC — either to another HC or to the SC itself. This can be done suo motu, on AG's application, or on a party's application.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Art. 142 operates on matters already pending before the SC to ensure complete justice — it does not govern inter-HC or HC-to-SC transfers.
• Option (b) — Correct: Art. 139A is precisely the provision designed for this scenario — multiple HCs deciding the same constitutional challenge divergently. Transferring them to the SC ensures uniformity.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Art. 131 covers governmental federal disputes (Centre-State / State-State), not constitutional challenges filed by citizens or private parties.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Art. 136 SLP is filed after a HC has delivered judgment — the scenario involves cases still pending before HCs.

Value Addition:
• Art. 139A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) — a notable origin during the Emergency period.
• The AG's standing to apply under Art. 139A reflects the Centre's interest in constitutional uniformity.
• Once transferred to the SC, the case is heard de novo or from the stage of transfer, depending on SC's direction.

solution.concept_anchor: Prospective overruling doctrine — SC not bound by its own decisions

statement_analysis.statement: The ratio decidendi of a Supreme Court judgment constitutes binding law under Article 141, but the Supreme Court itself can overrule its own earlier decisions through a larger bench, as it is not bound by Article 141 in the same manner as subordinate courts.
statement_analysis.reason: This is settled constitutional law — Art. 141 binds all courts including HCs, but the SC can revisit its own decisions through a larger bench or Constitution Bench. The SC is not self-bound by its own precedents.

statement_analysis.statement: The doctrine of prospective overruling, as applied in the Golak Nath case (1967), allows the Supreme Court to declare a new legal principle applicable only to future cases while protecting past transactions based on the overruled law.
statement_analysis.reason: The Golak Nath case introduced prospective overruling into Indian jurisprudence — the SC held that its new ruling (on parliamentary power to amend FRs) would apply only prospectively, not disturbing past constitutional amendments.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 141 applies only to judgments delivered by a Full Bench of the Supreme Court comprising at least five judges; decisions of smaller benches of two or three judges are persuasive but not binding on High Courts.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 141 makes no distinction based on bench size — even a two-judge SC bench's decision is binding on all courts under Art. 141. The five-judge requirement under Art. 145(3) applies only to constitutional interpretation questions, not to the binding nature of SC decisions generally.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may accept Statement 2 as incorrect because they confuse 'prospective overruling' with 'overruling' generally, thinking any overruling by a larger bench disturbs past decisions — making them doubt Statement 2's correctness.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: SC not self-bound + larger bench can overrule = correct; not an error.
Statement 2: Golak Nath case (1967) did introduce prospective overruling in India — correct; not an error.
Statement 3: Art. 141 makes no bench-size distinction; a two-judge SC ruling is as binding as a five-judge ruling — this statement imposes a false threshold; incorrect.
Only Statement 3 is NOT correct — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 deploys the scope-extension trap by importing the Art. 145(3) five-judge requirement (for constitutional questions) into the Art. 141 binding precedent rule. These are two entirely separate provisions with different purposes. Students who know 'five judges = Constitution Bench = important decisions' may conflate this with 'only five-judge decisions are binding.' In reality, every SC decision, regardless of bench size, is binding on all subordinate courts under Art. 141.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 141's binding precedent rule and the SC's internal practice of overruling through larger benches are both critical dimensions of judicial hierarchy.

• Statement 1 — Correct (not the error): Art. 141 binds all subordinate courts but the SC is not self-bound — a larger bench can overrule a smaller bench's precedent. This is the mechanism of constitutional evolution.
• Statement 2 — Correct (not the error): The Golak Nath case (1967) is the foundational case for prospective overruling in India — the SC applied its holding on parliamentary amendment power only to future cases, protecting past amendments.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect (the error): Art. 141 draws no distinction based on bench composition. Even a single SC judge's order on an urgent matter, or a two-judge Division Bench's judgment, is binding on all HCs and subordinate courts. The five-judge threshold in Art. 145(3) governs which bench must hear constitutional questions — it does not define which decisions are binding.

Value Addition:
• Kesavananda Bharati (1973) by a 13-judge bench modified Golak Nath's ruling on parliamentary amendment power.
• India adopted prospective overruling from US constitutional jurisprudence.
• The concept of 'per incuriam' decisions — SC rulings made without noticing a binding precedent — are not binding even on HCs.

solution.concept_anchor: Distinguished jurist — never used; retirement age 65 under Art. 124(2)

statement_analysis.statement: The 'distinguished jurist' route for appointment to the Supreme Court under Article 124(3)(c) has never been used in the history of the Indian Republic, though it remains a constitutionally valid eligibility path.
statement_analysis.reason: No appointment to the SC has ever been made through the distinguished jurist route since 1950 — the route exists in the Constitution but has remained practically dormant.

statement_analysis.statement: Supreme Court judges are required to retire at the age of 62 years, the same retirement age applicable to High Court judges.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 124(2) fixes the retirement age of SC judges at 65 years; the HC judges' retirement age under Article 217(1) is 62 years — these are distinct and different retirement ages.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the distinguished jurist route has never been used may accept Statement 1 as correct but, conflating SC and HC retirement ages, also accept Statement 2 as correct (remembering '62 years' from their HC study without distinguishing it from SC's 65).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Distinguished jurist route under Art. 124(3)(c) is constitutionally valid but has never been invoked — correct.
Statement 2: SC retirement age is 65 (Art. 124(2)); HC retirement age is 62 (Art. 217(1)) — the statement conflates the two; incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a partial-truth trap: the number '62 years' is correct for HC judges, creating a sense of recognition in the student. The trap is that SC and HC retirement ages are different — 65 vs. 62 respectively. Students who associate '62 years' with 'Supreme Court judges' (perhaps because HCs are discussed more often in practice) will accept Statement 2. The UPSC has tested this retirement age distinction multiple times.
solution.final_explanation:
Two independent facts about SC judges — the unused distinguished jurist route and the retirement age — are tested here.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The distinguished jurist route (Art. 124(3)(c)) has existed since 1950 but has never been used. No appointment through this route has occurred in over 70 years of constitutional history, unlike the UK and USA where equivalent routes are actively used.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: SC judges retire at 65 years under Art. 124(2). High Court judges retire at 62 years under Art. 217(1). These are deliberately different retirement ages — conflating them is a classic UPSC-tested error.

Value Addition:
• The retirement age for SC judges (65) is higher than that for HC judges (62), reflecting the SC's senior constitutional position.
• Before the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963, HC judges had no fixed retirement age by constitutional provision.
• The President is the formal authority who determines 'distinguished jurist' eligibility under Art. 124(3)(c) — a subjective, non-reviewable determination.

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 129, 215, 139A, 222 — contempt, record status, transfer provisions
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Art. 215 gives HCs court-of-record status may match it with 'Contempt power of HCs' while also swapping Art. 139A with Art. 222, particularly because both involve 'transfers.'
elimination_logic: A: Art. 129 — SC is a court of record, with inherent power to punish contempt of itself; matches with '3'.
B: Art. 215 — HC is a court of record with power to punish for contempt of itself; matches with '1'.
C: Art. 139A — Transfer of cases (not judges) involving common questions of law from one HC to another or to SC; matches with '4'.
D: Art. 222 — Transfer of HC judges by President after consultation with CJI; matches with '2'.
Correct: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap in this match-the-column operates between Art. 139A (case transfer) and Art. 222 (judge transfer). Both involve 'transfer' in the context of the judicial system, and students who do not carefully distinguish which article transfers what will swap them. Separately, students sometimes attribute the HC's court-of-record power to Art. 226 rather than Art. 215, creating another potential swap between B entries.
solution.final_explanation:
Four critical articles define the SC and HC's institutional powers and the transfer mechanisms.

Correct pairings:
• A — Article 129 (List entry 3): Declares the SC a court of record with inherent contempt power — the foundational independence provision for the apex court.
• B — Article 215 (List entry 1): Confers identical court-of-record and contempt status on every HC — the HC's structural equivalent of Art. 129.
• C — Article 139A (List entry 4): Empowers the SC to transfer cases (not judges) involving common legal questions between HCs or from HC to SC — prevents contradictory decisions.
• D — Article 222 (List entry 2): Governs the transfer of HC judges by the President, with CJI consultation — distinct from case transfers under Art. 139A.

The primary trap: Art. 139A = cases transferred; Art. 222 = judges transferred. The secondary trap: Art. 215 (not Art. 226) gives HCs court-of-record status.

Value Addition:
• Both Art. 129 (SC) and Art. 215 (HC) create courts of record — their records are evidentiary and unquestionable.
• Art. 222 transfers require CJI's effective concurrence post-Third Judges Case (1998).
• The truth-as-defence amendment (2006) to the Contempt of Courts Act applies to both SC and HC contempt proceedings.

solution.concept_anchor: Impeachment failure (Ramaswami 1993) — convention vs. constitutional mandate
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion correct? Yes: No judge of the Supreme Court has ever been successfully impeached or removed in independent India's history — the Ramaswami motion (1993) failed in Lok Sabha.

Step 2 — Is Reason correct? Yes: The impeachment process requires special majority (total membership + 2/3rds present and voting) in both Houses in the same session — this is an unusually high threshold.

Step 3 — Does R explain A? No: R correctly describes the procedural difficulty (high special majority), but the Ramaswami case failed not because of the mathematical majority threshold being unmet — the Rajya Sabha passed the motion — but because the ruling Congress party chose to abstain in Lok Sabha, a political rather than mathematical failure. R is a plausible but incomplete causal explanation; more precisely, R explains why impeachment is structurally difficult, not why no judge has been removed specifically.
Both A and R are correct; R is a true contributory factor but not the complete or exclusive causal explanation — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This assertion-reason exploits the reversed-causation trap. Students who know both facts — (A) no judge removed, (R) high threshold required — instinctively link them as cause and effect. However, the Ramaswami case's failure was primarily political (Congress abstention), not mathematical. R is a structural reason why removal is difficult, but it does not fully causally explain A. The nuance is that 'R is a contributing factor' does not qualify as 'R is the correct explanation of A' in the UPSC assertion-reason framework.
solution.final_explanation:
The impeachment process's perfect non-use record and the procedural threshold are both constitutional facts, but the causal link between them is nuanced.

A — Correct: No SC judge has been successfully removed in India's constitutional history. The Justice V. Ramaswami case (1993) is the closest attempt — Rajya Sabha passed the motion but it failed in Lok Sabha when the ruling Congress party abstained.
R — Correct: The special majority requirement (majority of total membership + 2/3rd present and voting in each House in the same session) is among the most demanding thresholds in the Constitution.
Causal connection: While R describes a genuine structural barrier, it is not the complete causal explanation for A. The Ramaswami case failed due to political abstention, not because the mathematical threshold was mathematically impossible to achieve. R explains structural difficulty; it does not fully explain the specific historical outcome.

Both correct, R not the exclusive explanation — option (b).

Value Addition:
• The Judges Inquiry Act 1968 requires investigation before Parliament votes — adding further procedural layers.
• Even if both Houses pass the address, Presidential concurrence is required for removal to take effect.
• Justice Soumitra Sen (Calcutta HC) faced impeachment proceedings in 2011 — resigned before Lok Sabha voted.

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 226 wider subject matter than Art. 32 — 'any other purpose' phrase
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Art. 32 is a Fundamental Right while Art. 226 is not may incorrectly conclude that Art. 32 therefore has wider legal power than Art. 226, reversing the actual subject-matter scope relationship.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Art. 32 cannot be used for enforcement of rights other than Fundamental Rights — so a violation of a statutory right cannot be remedied under Art. 32 directly.
Eliminate (b): Art. 32 being a FR means it has constitutional status — but this does not mean its subject-matter scope is wider than Art. 226. The two provisions serve different purposes.
Eliminate (c): HCs have no power under Art. 226 to issue writs against the Supreme Court or to question its decisions — that is a jurisdictional limitation.

Confirm (d): Article 226 includes the phrase 'for any other purpose' beyond FR enforcement — meaning HCs can issue writs for violation of statutory rights, legal rights, or public law duties, making Art. 226's subject-matter scope broader than Art. 32's FR-only scope.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap operates by making students conflate 'constitutional status' with 'wider scope of application.' Art. 32 is a FR (higher constitutional status), but Art. 226 has wider subject-matter jurisdiction ('any other purpose'). Students who reason 'FR > non-FR, therefore Art. 32 > Art. 226 in scope' commit a category error — constitutional hierarchy and subject-matter breadth are distinct dimensions.
solution.final_explanation:
The comparison between Art. 32 and Art. 226 has multiple dimensions — constitutional status, subject-matter scope, and hierarchical authority.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Art. 32 is limited to FR enforcement; it cannot be invoked for violations of statutory rights alone.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: While Art. 32 is itself a FR (which Art. 226 is not), this constitutional status does not translate into wider subject-matter scope. Art. 32's scope is FR-only; Art. 226's scope is FRs plus 'any other purpose.'
• Option (c) — Incorrect: High Courts cannot issue writs questioning the SC's decisions or the SC itself — the SC is hierarchically above all HCs.
• Option (d) — Correct: Article 226's express inclusion of 'any other purpose' beyond FR enforcement is what makes its subject-matter scope wider than Art. 32. An HC can grant relief for violation of contractual rights, statutory rights, and administrative law principles under Art. 226.

Value Addition:
• Despite Art. 226's wider scope, Art. 32's status as a FR itself means it cannot be excluded by ordinary law; Art. 226 can be restricted.
• PIL jurisdiction has been developed primarily under Art. 32 at the SC level and Art. 226 at the HC level.
• HC writs under Art. 226 are subject to territorial jurisdiction; SC writs under Art. 32 have pan-India reach.
